similar_scenes.name: Vídeos y cine: de The Song Remains the Same a Spinal Tap
similar_scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
similar_scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
similar_scenes.desc: Fuera de MTV el vídeo es un medio especializado que los fans compran: recopilaciones (Fuel for Life de Judas Priest), conciertos (Live After Death de Iron Maiden), documentales al modo de The Song Remains the Same de Led Zeppelin, cintas-revista y promociones de sellos independientes de thrash como Combat y Metal Blade. Metallica deconstruye el formato con Cliff ’em All, homenaje a Cliff Burton hecho con grabaciones caseras y piratas. El cine, que necesita un público de masas, apenas trata el metal, salvo como banda sonora de películas de terror. Las dos películas sobre él de los ochenta, This Is Spinal Tap (1984), la parodia de Rob Reiner, y The Decline of Western Civilization Part II: The Metal Years (1988) de Penelope Spheeris, dan placer al público metal pero aún más a sus detractores: una es una crítica cultural de la falta de sofisticación; la otra, una crítica moral de la depravación, estrenada tras los ataques del PMRC. Spinal Tap acabó saliendo de gira de verdad.

podcast.title: Growth During Musicians' Strike (1942)
podcast.body: Western performers, like country musicians, were not subject to the American Federation of Musicians strike in 1942 because ACAPE did not classify them as "real musicians." This exemption allowed them to continue recording and disseminating their music rapidly at a time when Big Band recordings were restricted. "Acape also did not consider country musicians, western performers, and R&B acts to be real musicians. As a result, they were not covered by any prohibitions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Slicker" Sound in the 1930s-40s
podcast.body: In the 1930s and 40s, Western music was notably "slicker" than country music, influenced by the "Hollywoodization" of the genre. This period saw the rise of singing cowboy films starring figures like Gene Autry and Roy Rogers, which introduced elements such as crooning and orchestras into the music. "And at the time we're talking about the 30s and 40s, it was a little bit slicker than Country music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 3: "Ida Red" by Bob Wills and the Texas Playboys

podcast.title: Geographic and Thematic Characteristics
podcast.body: Western music originated in Texas, Oklahoma, and California, featuring subject matter largely focused on cowboys and outlaws. It often employed similar instrumentation to country music, such as violins and guitars, but developed a distinct identity. "That was the music being made in Texas, Oklahoma and California, and it tended to use similar instrumentation to country music, violins and guitars and so on."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 3: "Ida Red" by Bob Wills and the Texas Playboys

podcast.title: Increased Radio Exposure (WWII Era)
podcast.body: As radio programming shifted to more cost-effective record playbacks and local stations gained more evening autonomy, Western records found increased airtime. This new exposure introduced the genre to wider audiences alongside country, hillbilly, and R&B. "But it also made room for country, western, hillbilly, and R&B records. People started to hear other genres on the radio for the very first time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
